source.title: Scaling Laws for Associative Memories
source.authors: Vivien Cabannes; Elvis Dohmatob; A. Bietti

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or cutoff; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives and evaluates scaling relationships in a simplified associative-memory model, using 0-1 generalization error rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The reported scaling results concern a toy associative-memory model and its 0-1 generalization error, not language-model pretraining loss. The paper does not test extrapolation of language-model loss, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, architecture-shape effects in language models, other modalities, or downstream task performance. Its optimization experiments are on the toy model.
record.test_reason: The paper derives scaling laws for a toy outer-product associative-memory model, measured as 0-1 generalization error on Zipf-distributed discrete tokens. It offers a theory of why scaling laws might arise and cites Kaplan and Hoffmann. It trains no language model and measures no held-out pretraining loss, so none of its results bear directly on V1–V7. The record's 'tests/T2' contradicts its own per-version 'not_tested' statuses. Treat this as a theoretical discussion study whose toy-model findings belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors derive data and capacity scaling laws for a simple associative-memory model of memorization in transformers and find uniformly weighted outer products best. They report that small batches and large learning rates help, and that Adam and layer norm help under practical constraints. They propose richer transformer-like models as future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes a simplified associative-memory model with random token embeddings and 0-1 generalization error, rather than language-model pretraining runs and held-out cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: In the toy model, scaling and performance differ with memory weighting scheme, threshold P, embedding training, nonlinearities, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and layer normalization.

fits_no_version.finding: In a Zipf-data associative-memory toy model, error scales as T^{-1+1/α}+d^{-α+1} under optimal thresholding. The capacity exponent depends on the storage scheme: d^{-(α-1)/2α} for q=p.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy associative memories with Zipf-distributed tokens, error follows power laws in data and capacity, with exponents set by the data tail and the storage scheme.

fits_no_version.finding: Finite support N produces a tipping point to zero error. Optimizer choice, learned embeddings or nonlinearity change the constant, the tipping point or the exponent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy memory models, training and representation choices alter the shape and exponent of capacity scaling curves.

record.problems: The evidence concerns a simplified associative-memory model, not language models. Several reported experimental comparisons are presented only in figures, and numerical values are not tabulated. The paper's theoretical results rely on specified Zipf-distribution and embedding assumptions.

untested.parts: No LM held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No depth/width comparisons at fixed LM parameter count.
No other modalities or LM training regimes.
Exponent dependence on scheme and optimizer is shown only in a toy memory model, not in fitted LM laws.

missing.what: Effects of step size, batch size, Adam and layer norm on toy-model error versus d. Fig. 7 shows large step size, small batch, Adam and LN improving error.
Larger-N check that the q=p and thresholded curves follow the predicted d^{-1/4} and d^{-1} slopes.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts are given because no LM scaling-law version is tested. The paper links its rates to Hutter (2021) and Michaud et al. (2023) as possible explanations of LLM scaling, but this is argument rather than an LM test.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy in language models.
No small-run fit is used to predict loss on much larger language-model runs.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation or compute-optimal trend is measured.
The paper does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed language-model parameter count.
No other modalities or language-model training regimes are tested.
No downstream task performance is measured.
The paper varies memory schemes and toy-model training choices, but does not test fitted language-model exponents, compute-optimal allocations, or language-model curves bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: infinite memory model

rows.note: The text states the scaling up to constant factors.
rows.check: This is a theoretical rate for a toy infinite-memory model, not LM loss. 'observed' has no version to be judged against; it is better read as the derived result holding in the toy setting.

rows.uncertainty: Figure 3 reports averages over 100 runs; no numerical error bar value stated.
rows.note: The finite-N behavior includes a capacity tipping region rather than a single power-law decline across the full plotted range.

rows.subject: associative memory model optimized by optimization-based algorithms
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimization-based training with hand-designed schemes as capacity varies.
rows.value: The caption states that the optimization-based curves have a similar exponent, a smaller constant, and an earlier tipping point; exact values are figure only.
rows.note: The text says the curves appear to retain the optimal exponent d^{-α+1}; exact plotted values are not tabulated.
rows.check: This compares optimizer-trained toy memories with hand-designed schemes (Fig. 12 left). It is a toy-model method comparison, not a claim-version result.

rows.subject: associative memory model with learned input embeddings or nonlinear model
rows.stage_stated: embeddings learned; Figure 12 uses 10^3 updates and batch size 10^3
rows.operation_detail: Compared learning the matrix alone with learning embeddings, and with a nonlinear ReLU model.

conditions.value: N=100 in Figure 12; N=100 and d=2 in Figure 8

rows.value: The text and caption report that learning embeddings or using the nonlinear model improves storage, with a better exponent in d and an earlier zero-error tipping point; exact values are figure only.
rows.locator: Figure 8; Figure 12, middle and right panels
rows.note: Figure 8 reports zero generalization error at d=2 for the learned-embedding setting.
rows.check: This compares learned embeddings and a ReLU model with learning W alone in the toy model. Fig. 8 uses d=2 and M=5 or 10; the zero-error result is shown in Fig. 8 and Fig. 12 right.
